etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lenen (“to lean”), from Old English hleonian, hlinian (“to lean, recline, lie down, rest”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlinēn, from Proto-Germanic *hlināną (“to lean, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.

Cognate via Proto-Germanic with Middle Dutch leunen (“to lean”), German lehnen (“to lean”); via Proto-Indo-European with climate, cline.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To incline, deviate, or bend, from a vertical position; to be in a position thus inclining or deviating.
(copulative) To incline in opinion or desire; to conform in conduct; often with to, toward, etc.

quote.citation: a. 1600, Edmund Spenser, “A View of the State of Ireland. […]”, in The Works of Mr. Edmund Spenser, volume VI, London: Jacob Tonson […], published 1715, →OCLC, page 1518:
quote.text: But you ſay they do not accept of them, but delight rather to lean to their old Cuſtoms and Brehon Laws, though they be more unjuſt and alſo more inconvenient for the common People, as by your late Relation of them I have gathered.

definitions.definition: (Followed by against, on, or upon) To rest or rely, for support, comfort, etc.

quote.citation: 1864, Alfred Tennyson, “Aylmer’s Field”, in Enoch Arden, &c., London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 54:
quote.text: He lean'd not on his fathers but himself.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XLV, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC, pages 374–375:
quote.text: The slightest effort made the patient cough. He would stand leaning on a stick and holding a hand to his side, and when the paroxysm had passed it left him shaking.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Tenth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 533, lines 1187–1188:
quote.text: Oppreſs'd with Anguiſh, panting, and o'reſpent, / His fainting Limbs against an Oak he leant.

definitions.definition: (of an object taller than its width and depth) An inclination away from the vertical.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English lene (“lean”), from Old English hlǣne (“lean”), (cognate with Low German leen), perhaps from hlǣnan (“to cause to lean (due to hunger or lack of food)”), from Proto-Germanic *hlainijaną (“to cause to lean”). If so, then related to Old English hlinian, hleonian (“to lean”).

definitions.definition: (of a person or animal) Slim; not fleshy.

quote.citation: 2024 January 5, ZacharyFurr, “Gym types”, in The In Constant Chronicles‎[1]:
quote.text: They will now dedicate several hours at the gym every day to be leaner and stronger.

quote.citation: 2007, Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, Penguin, →ISBN, page 34:
quote.text: The butcher and the porkman painted up only the leanest scrags of meat; the baker, the coarsest of meagre loaves.

definitions.definition: Having little extra or little to spare; scanty; meagre.
Having a low proportion or concentration of a desired substance or ingredient.
(printing, archaic) Of a character which prevents the compositor from earning the usual wages; opposed to fat.
(business) Efficient, economic, frugal, agile, slimmed-down; pertaining to the modern industrial principles of "lean manufacturing".

quote.citation: 2007, Richard J. Schonberger, Best Practices in Lean Six Sigma Process Improvement, page 204:
quote.text: Kitting for in-plant handling is unlean. Kitting for transport, on the other hand, is lean; for example, shipping complete sets of parts to make a TV or motorcycle or motor home is lean.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Meat with no fat on it.

quote.text: Jack Sprat would eat no fat, / His wife would eat no lean.

definitions.definition: (countable, biology) An organism that is lean in stature.

quote.text: The intermediates and leans are the predominant morphotypes found at the SE-NHR seamounts  […]

quote.citation: 2012, Obesity: New Insights for the Healthcare Professional, page 56:
quote.text: Obese Zuckers, compared to leans, consumed more food under free-feeding conditions.

definitions.definition: To thin out (a fuel-air mixture): to reduce the fuel flow into the mixture so that there is more air or oxygen.

quote.citation: 1938 July, Harold Blaine Miller, Dupont Miller, “Weather Hop”, in Boys' Life‎[2], Boy Scouts of America, →ISSN, page 25:
quote.text: He leaned the mixture in an effort to cause a backfire through the carburetor, the generally accepted method of breaking the ice loose.

quote.citation: 2002 July, Tom Benenson, “Can Your Engine Run Too Lean?”, in Flying‎[3], volume 129, number 7, →ISSN, page 73:
quote.text: Even the Pilot's Operating Handbooks (POH) for our training airplanes add to our paranoia with their insistence that we not lean the mixture until we're above 5000 feet density altitude.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Icelandic leyna? Akin to German leugnen (“deny”). Compare lie (“speak falsely”).

definitions.definition: (Can we verify(+) this sense?) To conceal.[1]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably from the verb to lean (see etymology 1 above), supposedly because consumption of the intoxicating beverage causes one to "lean". Alternatively, possibly short for gasoline (“an alcoholic beverage made of vodka and energy drink”).

definitions.definition: (slang, US) A recreational drug based on codeine-laced promethazine cough syrup, especially popular in the hip hop community in the southeastern United States.

quote.citation: 2005, “Stay Fly”, in Jordan Houston, Darnell Carlton, Paul Beauregard, Premro Smith, Marlon Goodwin, David Brown, Willie Hutchinson (lyrics), Most Known Unknown‎[4], performed by Three 6 Mafia (featuring Young Buck, 8 Ball, and MJG), Sony BMG:
quote.text: Eyes real tight 'cause I'm chokin' the creep; vision messed up 'cause I'm drinkin' the lean.

quote.citation: 2020, “Those Kinda Nights”, in Music to Be Murdered By, performed by Eminem ft. Ed Sheeran:
quote.text: "What's in the cup, let me see that / Girl, where the rest of that promethazine at?" / She said, "Cool, gotta run out to my Cadillac though / And I'll be like Fat Joe, and bring the lean back"
